## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no results yet, and scores stay hidden for the whole search, so I have to rely on what the task's structure suggests. The default recipe gives only about 32 PPO updates of 4,096 samples each, which is very few policy-improvement steps. Smaller rollouts and slightly fewer epochs should raise sample efficiency. To score a placement, the agent has to know the landing layer (the maximum build height under the footprint) and which target cells sit at that layer in each footprint cell. The starting head only sees max, min and average over the footprint, not which value sits in which footprint cell. Also, the network only sees a 5x5 neighbourhood and has no global context. Round 1 tests three things: the recipe alone on the starting network, a footprint-convolution head with global context, and a cell-attention network. All three keep the compute ratio r at about 1.5 or less, so few training samples are lost.

### Round 2
All three round-1 trials trained without errors, but scores are hidden, so I can't rank them. All I know is that the baseline, the footprint-conv head and the attention trunk all fit the time limit. They also all pass the rule checks. So this round goes for variety instead of chasing one result, and each candidate makes one clear change. (1) Refinement: r1c2 with a deeper trunk that uses dilation. On an 8x8 grid this lets every cell see the whole board, which matters for overhangs and build order. (2) Recipe: r1c2 with fewer PPO epochs, which buys more fresh samples, plus a higher GAE lambda for the delayed exact-build bonus. (3) New idea: a layer-wise network. It scores each placement at each height layer, with shared 2D convs over a window of z-1, z and z+1. A learned soft gate over layers then picks the landing layer. This matches how the task works: what matters is which layer a brick lands on and which cells it fills there.

### Round 3
Scores are hidden, so the only evidence is that every file trained without errors. I am reasoning from the budget and the task structure. Each trial gets only about 100k to 200k samples, and every episode draws a fresh design, so the number of samples probably matters a lot. Networks with r above about 1.3 trade away many samples (r1c3, r2c1 and r2c3 got 92k to 110k), which is risky. The footprint head (r1c2) is the most task-aligned and cheap design. Recipes that cut PPO epochs to get more samples look good. This round I keep r near 1.2 and push in three directions. First, the r2c2 recipe with less entropy and a longer horizon, so that greedy evaluation is sharper. Second, a slimmer but deeper dilated trunk whose receptive field covers the whole grid, at r about 1.2. Third, an extreme of 1 PPO epoch for about 340k samples.

### Round 4
No scores are visible, so I can only judge the trials by their design. All 8 trials trained without errors. The footprint-convolution head (r1c2) is the most direct way to see the cells under each footprint, so it is the base for every candidate here. Deeper trunks, attention and layer-wise scoring each raised r. That cuts the sample count, and since every episode uses a fresh random design, samples look like the scarce resource. Trials that kept r near 1.2 and used 1 to 2 PPO epochs (r2c2, r3c1, r3c3) seem the safest bets, but without scores I cannot rank them. With one round left I avoid risky architecture changes. I propose two low-variance recipe combinations that blend the sample-rich and low-entropy ideas, and one cheap network change: feeding the legal-action mask in as an input. The mask shows where the height limit blocks a placement, at almost no extra compute.
